I have a sign up that says "beware of dog". If my house is made of glass, you can see everything that's inside (my program) and how it works, but that doesn't get you around my big dog. Additionally, while you might be able to plan routes around the dog and try to infiltrate my house, everyone else in the community can also see those routes and try to shore them up before you can use them. People in the community can make suggestions like better door locks to make your infiltrating job even harder.

I have a sign up that says "beware of dog". My house is made of wood, and you can't see anything that's inside. This makes it harder to plan around the dog, but it also makes it harder for the community to plan around your actions as well. If you're very good at infiltrating houses, there's a good chance you'll be able to mitigate the dog situation regardless, and no one will see how you did it. Additionally, no one can see my dog, so it could be that I'm housing a chihuahua that poses little threat to a home intruder.

It's not a perfect analogy, so maybe someone can comment and improve it, but it's the gist of the argument of open source vs security through obscurity.
So basically your saying that while there still will be security holes, because the community can help, they get patched much faster?

That's the theory, and when implemented correctly it can mean well-secured software that doesn't require a huge monetary investment to sustain. The added benefit is that the community can suggest their own improvements to security (bigger dogs, more dogs, door locks, encrypted boxes for user data to reside in, etc.). You are also able to audit the open source code and see exactly how secure it is to begin with. When dealing with closed source software, you only have the software maker's word and reputation that the software is free from security holes. And with (comparatively) less eyes looking at the software, it's possible that there are security vulnerabilities that haven't been noticed yet, but can still be exploited by a persistent enough threat.

Frankly, stuff like heartbleed going undiscovered for 3 years is a perfect example why OSS isn't necessarily more secure.

The whole "lots of eyes" thing is predicated on the idea that lots of people are scrutinizing the code when that really isn't true. In order to live up to its promise we would have to expect more end users to be able to understand code, which is both naive and preposterous.

I agree with you. A theoretically sound system only works when the theory is followed, and heartbleed is a great example of a major security vulnerability that went unnoticed simply because no one was auditing the code. Major players used it and relied on it, but didn't give back to the open source community by checking the code for vulnerabilities, which is a cornerstone of the open source model. With heartbleed, that model lost its balance and more people were using the code than evaluating it, which made the eventual exploit much worse.
